claim: Cannabidiol reduces seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome
gold_rationale: Consensus is clearly Supported. Two independent double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 RCTs whose PRIMARY endpoint was exactly the claimed outcome (convulsive seizure frequency) both hit significance: GWPCARE1 (Devinsky, NEJM 2017, N=120, NCT02091375) showed the CBD group's median monthly convulsive seizures fall 12.4->5.9 vs 14.9->14.1 on placebo (adjusted median difference -22.8 percentage points, 95% CI -41.1 to -5.4, P=0.01), and GWPCARE2 (Miller, JAMA Neurology 2020, N=198, NCT02224703) showed placebo-adjusted reductions of 29.8% (P=.01) at 10 mg/kg/d and 25.7% (P=.03) at 20 mg/kg/d. Independent academic meta-analyses confirm robustness (Lattanzi 2020 CNS Drugs: pooled RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.21-2.36 for >=50%-responder; Devinsky 2020 Acta Neurol Scand: efficacious with AND without concomitant clobazam). The FDA approved purified cannabidiol (Epidiolex) for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome in patients >=2 years on 25-Jun-2018 (NDA 210365, granted to GW Research Ltd) — a formal regulatory endorsement of exactly this claim. Comparative network meta-analysis (Lattanzi 2023 Drugs) ranks CBD BELOW fenfluramine and stiripentol but still efficacious versus placebo — this affects relative ranking, not the truth of the claim. Direction of effect and outcome-match are unambiguous, so the claim is Supported.
outcome: Convulsive (and total) seizure frequency — reduction from baseline vs placebo
population: Children and young adults (age 2-18) with genetically/clinically confirmed Dravet syndrome and drug-resistant convulsive seizures, on >=1 background antiepileptic drug
provenance: PubMed get_article_metadata for all 7 PMIDs (titles, article_types, N, primary-endpoint text, retraction check) and ClinicalTrials.gov get_trial_details for NCT02091375 (GWPCARE1) and NCT02224703 (GWPCARE2) confirming PHASE3 design, enrollment, and convulsive-seizure-frequency PRIMARY endpoints. FDA approval (25-Jun-2018, NDA 210365, Dravet+LGS, >=2 years) verified via FDA approval letter and press release. All ids resolve to the cited articles/trials.
notes: Both pivotal RCTs measured the CLAIMED outcome directly (convulsive seizure frequency as PRIMARY endpoint per ClinicalTrials.gov and the published abstracts) — no surrogate substitution, so outcome_match=true is honest for rows 1 and 2. GWPCARE1 and GWPCARE2 ClinicalTrials.gov records now list Jazz Pharmaceuticals as sponsor (Jazz acquired GW Pharmaceuticals in 2021); original industry sponsor was GW Pharmaceuticals/GW Research. Industry funding noted as integrity consideration but does not undermine consensus given independent FDA review and independent academic meta-analyses (Lattanzi group has no industry sponsorship of the reviews). Row 4 (Acta Neurol Scand) pools 2 Dravet + 2 Lennox-Gastaut RCTs, so its population is mixed (population_match set false) though it remains supportive. Devinsky 2018 Neurology (PMID 29540584) is a real dose-ranging SAFETY/PK trial (N=34, Class I safety evidence, primary endpoint safety/PK not seizure frequency) and is deliberately EXCLUDED from the efficacy rows to avoid overcounting. No article in the corpus is a Retracted Publication.

baseline.text: Yes. Cannabidiol (Epidiolex) significantly reduces convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome. In the pivotal NEJM 2017 trial (Devinsky et al., N=120), CBD 20 mg/kg/day cut median monthly convulsive seizures from 12.4 to 5.9 versus essentially no change on placebo (14.9 to 14.1; adjusted difference -22.8 percentage points, P=0.01), and a second randomized trial (GWPCARE2, JAMA Neurology 2020) confirmed a ~30% placebo-adjusted reduction at 10 mg/kg/day. On the strength of these trials the FDA approved cannabidiol for Dravet syndrome in June 2018. It is an established, evidence-based adjunctive therapy, though it carries risks of somnolence, decreased appetite, elevated liver enzymes, and a drug interaction with clobazam.

rows.citation: Devinsky O, et al. Trial of Cannabidiol for Drug-Resistant Seizures in the Dravet Syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2017;376(21):2011-2020. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1611618 (NCT02091375, GWPCARE1)
rows.integrity_note: Pivotal double-blind placebo-controlled Phase 3 (confirmed PHASE3 on ClinicalTrials.gov); funded by GW Pharmaceuticals (industry) — peer-reviewed in NEJM and a basis for FDA approval. Not retracted.
rows.finding: Primary endpoint = change in convulsive-seizure frequency. Median monthly convulsive seizures fell 12.4->5.9 on CBD 20 mg/kg/d vs 14.9->14.1 on placebo; adjusted median difference -22.8 percentage points (95% CI -41.1 to -5.4; P=0.01). >=50% responder rate 43% vs 27% (OR 2.00; P=0.08). N=120 total (60 CBD / 60 placebo); n_int reflects the CBD arm.

rows.citation: Miller I, et al. Dose-Ranging Effect of Adjunctive Oral Cannabidiol vs Placebo on Convulsive Seizure Frequency in Dravet Syndrome (GWPCARE2): A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2020;77(5):613-621. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2020.0073 (NCT02224703)
rows.integrity_note: Second independent pivotal Phase 3 RCT (confirmed PHASE3 on ClinicalTrials.gov); industry-funded (GW Research/Greenwich Biosciences) but pre-registered, ITT-analyzed, peer-reviewed. Not retracted.
rows.finding: Primary endpoint = change from baseline in convulsive seizure frequency. Placebo-adjusted reduction 29.8% (95% CI 8.4-46.2; P=.01) for 10 mg/kg/d and 25.7% (95% CI 2.9-43.2; P=.03) for 20 mg/kg/d. N=198 (66 CBD10 / 67 CBD20 / 65 placebo); n_int reflects the two CBD arms combined. 10 mg/kg/d had better tolerability.

rows.citation: Lattanzi S, et al. Adjunctive Cannabidiol in Patients with Dravet Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Efficacy and Safety. CNS Drugs. 2020;34(3):229-241. doi:10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6
rows.integrity_note: Independent academic systematic review + meta-analysis (no industry sponsorship of the review); pooled 3 placebo-controlled Dravet RCTs. Not retracted.
rows.finding: Pooled 3 RCTs (359 participants; 228 CBD, 131 placebo). Pooled RR for >=50% reduction in convulsive seizure frequency = 1.69 (95% CI 1.21-2.36; P=0.002), favoring CBD. Higher withdrawal (RR 3.12) and AE profile with CBD (somnolence, decreased appetite, diarrhea, raised aminotransferases).

rows.citation: Devinsky O, et al. Cannabidiol efficacy independent of clobazam: Meta-analysis of four randomized controlled trials. Acta Neurol Scand. 2020;142(6):531-540. doi:10.1111/ane.13305
rows.integrity_note: Author overlap with GW/Greenwich (industry authors). Addresses the key confound that CBD's benefit might be a clobazam drug-drug-interaction artifact. population_match=false because the pool mixes 2 Dravet AND 2 Lennox-Gastaut RCTs (not a pure Dravet population). Not retracted.
rows.finding: Stratified meta-analysis of 4 RCTs (2 Dravet, 2 Lennox-Gastaut) shows CBD reduces seizure frequency vs placebo both WITH clobazam (treatment ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.52-0.68, P<.0001) and WITHOUT clobazam (0.85, 95% CI 0.73-0.98, P=.0226); 50% responder OR 2.51 (with CLB) and 2.40 (without CLB). Effect is not solely a clobazam interaction.

rows.citation: Lattanzi S, et al. Pharmacotherapy for Dravet Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Drugs. 2023;83(15):1409-1424. doi:10.1007/s40265-023-01936-y
rows.integrity_note: Independent network meta-analysis; provides comparative-effectiveness context — CBD is efficacious but ranks below fenfluramine and stiripentol on the claimed outcome. Does not contradict the claim vs placebo. Not retracted.
rows.finding: NMA of 8 placebo-controlled RCTs (680 patients; CBD arm n=228). Pharmaceutical-grade CBD is efficacious for >=50% convulsive-seizure response but had a LOWER response rate than fenfluramine (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.07-0.54); stiripentol had a HIGHER response rate than CBD (OR 14.07, 95% CI 2.57-76.87). CBD superior to placebo; comparatively less effective than the other two agents.

rows.citation: Gaston TE, Szaflarski JP. Cannabis for the Treatment of Epilepsy: an Update. Curr Neurol Neurosci Rep. 2018;18(11):73. doi:10.1007/s11910-018-0882-y
rows.integrity_note: Narrative expert review (PubMed type 'Review') used as the regulatory-action row documenting the June 2018 FDA approval of purified CBD for Dravet syndrome. FDA action independently confirmed via NDA 210365 approval letter (25-Jun-2018, >=2 years, GW Research Ltd). Not a primary guideline document, but content is accurate. Not retracted.
rows.finding: Purified oral CBD (Epidiolex) received FDA approval (25-Jun-2018, NDA 210365) for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in patients >=2 years, based on RCTs showing significant convulsive-seizure-frequency reduction vs placebo. Main AEs diarrhea, sedation (worse with clobazam), transaminase elevation (worse with valproate); notable CBD-clobazam CYP2C19 interaction increasing N-desmethylclobazam.
